newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS to meet in Tokyo, grapples with EMU effects.
newsitem.headline: BIS to meet in Tokyo, grapples with EMU effects.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) will continue to become more global in coming years and in 1998 its board will meet in Tokyo, the first time in its history a meeting is held outside Europe.

But while BIS is likely to add further new members from emerging markets in coming years, Europe will dominate the immediate agenda as the world's oldest international financial institution adapts to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), monetary sources said.
BIS's annual meeting takes place on Monday in Basle with central bank governors from around 100 countries gathering this weekend for an event that is part business, part social.

Illustrating the growing atttention paid to emerging states, governors from these countries will also discuss capital flows and financial liberalisation, and exchange views on how Thailand or the Czech Republic, for example, tackled the recent attacks on their currencies.

BIS, just like other international institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and the Group of Seven (G7), is grappling with the consequences of many of Europe's central banks likely joining in the European Central Bank (ECB).
The globalisation of BIS' membership and activities is one response to the changes in Europe.
But it is also clearly unsustainable for many European central banks to join into a single unit and still retain their individual seats in international bodies, such as BIS.

European governments have yet to come up with a plan for their future role in international institutions, but bankers doubt a solution will be found until there is clarity over the future of Europe's single currency.
BIS' board consists of central bank governors from the Group of 10 (G10): U.S., Japan, Canada, Germany, France, Italy, Britain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Switzerland.

BIS, founded in 1930 and for years dominated by Europeans, has gradually transformed itself into a worldwide institution, reflecting the growing economic and political clout of emerging markets and the global nature of bank cooperation.
It symbolised this change last year by asking nine new central banks to join; China, Russia, India, Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Mexico.
Other countries that economists have tipped as likely future members include Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Argentina.

The planned board meeting in Tokyo in July 1998 is another symbol of BIS' transformation, which is not only affecting the institutional structure, but also the issues discussed by central bank governors and experts.

Some of BIS's committees, for example, the Euro-currency Standing Committee, are considering meeting in Asia and BIS will deepen its relations with regional groups, such as the Latin American Centre for Monetary Studies (CEMLA) or Executive Meeting of East Asian and Pacific Central Banks (EMEAP).

Given the increasing weight of Asian countries in BIS, which provides financial services to around 100 central banks, sources speculate BIS could open a representative office in Asia to be in regular contact with its customers, which span the globe and operate in different timezones.
BIS' growing involvement with emerging markets is also reflected in its activities as a bank for central banks.
Deposits from European central banks are now less than half of BIS's total currency and gold deposits of some $120 billion, with Asian banks accounting for a substantial part.

Growing business with emerging markets will also help BIS, like other commercial banks, counter any expected decline in fees from foreing exchange transactions when Europe's single currency comes to life.
